newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin backs govt programme, explains NATO deal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin backs govt programme, explains NATO deal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin approved his reformist government's economic programme on Monday, despite warnings it will be tough on ordinary Russians, and tried to defuse communist opposition to a security pact with NATO.

Yeltsin enthusiastically supported the short-term economic measures at a meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, First Deputy Premiers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov and Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev.

"This is not a declaration, not just statistics, but rather a business document which addresses every problem facing each Russian and the country as a whole," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.

The seven-point plan contained no new policies but confirmed a trend towards deeper market reforms. It also outlined the aims of the cabinet, which two months ago replaced a more conservative team that had failed to end huge wage and pension arrears.

Chernomyrdin made paying these debts to public sector workers his top priority. He has said repeatedly he will pay off all the debts this summer in the face of warnings by critics who say the unpaid workers' patience has its limits.
He pledged to target help to those who really need it -- meaning cutting and restructuring subsidies.

He also vowed to secure an increase in industrial output, revive agriculture through cheap credits, support local initiatives from the centre, cut away at the roots of corruption and teach the state to live honestly, within its means.
"These policies are tough but essential for all our citizens," Chernomyrdin told a news conference.
He added: "The government will prove by its actions that it can carry out the plan outlined by President Boris Yeltsin."
Yeltsin added the seventh point -- committing the government to more openness and obliging it to explain all its moves to the media and general public.

Chernomyrdin and Chubais are due to brief the communist-led State Duma, the lower house of parliament, on Wednesday on the state of the economy in the first quarter and on their plan to cut spending by a fifth because of poor tax revenues.
The communists have said they will reject the government spending cuts, called a sequester, in a vote on Friday, but signs that a compromise is possible have emerged in the past few days.
Chernomyrdin said over the weekend that he might be open to cutting spending by less than forecast, an idea which a communist leader said last week might be acceptable.
"We hope the sequester will be passed. Probably it will not be (passed) immediately but there are things to work on," Chernomyrdin said, promising to work closely with the Duma.
After his talks with Chernomyrdin and the other ministers, Yeltsin briefed the speakers and party chiefs of both houses of parliament on last week's partnership deal between Russia and NATO.

The deal clears the way for Moscow and its former Cold War adversary to sign an agreement in Paris on May 27, mapping out their relations into the next century. These have been strained by a NATO plan, which Moscow opposes, to extend membership to former Soviet bloc states in Eastern Europe.

Yeltsin said he would review ties with NATO if the alliance ignored Russia's views. "If NATO begins to take decisions without taking account of Russia's opinion, Russia will review its relations with the alliance," he said.
He said Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, who negotiated the deal, would address a closed Duma session on Friday.

Yetsin's comments were clearly intended to appease communists and nationalists who oppose the agreement, although he does not need parliamentary approval, and to show them he will defend Russia's interests in relations with NATO.
